summary: Specifies new socket options and functions for multicast source filters. IGMPv3 and MLDv2 let receivers state which senders they will accept multicast traffic from, and this gives applications a programming interface to do so. It is informational.

eli5.summary: With group messages, you can say which senders you want to hear from and which to ignore. This document gives programmers the knobs in their code to say it.

questions: how to set source filters in igmpv3 programs
subtitle: The socket calls and options that let a program choose which senders it accepts multicast traffic from.

tldr.problem: IGMPv3 and MLDv2 let receivers filter multicast by sender, but the existing sockets API only lets an application name a group and an interface, not a list of sources.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds setsockopt() options for joining, leaving, blocking and unblocking individual sources, plus functions to set or get a complete source filter, with IPv4-specific and protocol-independent variants.
tldr.outcome: Existing multicast programs keep working unchanged, and new programs can detect when the source filter API is missing and fall back gracefully.

today: RFC 3678 is an Informational RFC and, per the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. The RFC itself says the official sockets API specification is POSIX, and treats the ioctl() forms in its appendix as historic.

sections.title: Why the Sockets API Needed Changes
sections.content:
The sockets interface is the de facto API for TCP/IP applications, and its users have enjoyed a high degree of portability. To keep that portability for programs that use multicast source filters, the sockets API has to change, and RFC 3678 describes the changes. It defines new socket options and functions to manage source filters for IP multicast group memberships, plus the structures used as their arguments.

RFC 3493 defines IPv6 socket extensions, including protocol-independent functions, but gives join and leave functions only for IPv6. This document adds protocol-independent versions. The RFC stresses that it is for informational purposes and that the official standard specification of the sockets API is POSIX.
sections.eli5: Programs talk to the network through a standard set of buttons called sockets. This paper adds a few new buttons so a program can pick which senders it wants to hear.

sections.title: Design Considerations
sections.content:
The design goals are compatible with old software. The changes must give both source and binary compatibility, so existing program binaries keep working and recompiled applications still work. They should be as small as possible, so converting a receiver application is easy. Applications should be able to detect that the new APIs are unavailable and react gracefully, for example by reverting to the old API or showing a meaningful error. Lack of type-safety should be avoided where possible.

Several implementations already used ioctl() for part of this, and Appendix A documents that for historical purposes. The preferred API uses new functions because they are type-safe, can be wrappers over an ioctl or setsockopt call, and can both pass information to the stack and retrieve it without changing getsockopt.
sections.eli5: The new buttons must not break old programs, must be easy to add, and a program should be able to tell if they are missing.

sections.title: Two Styles of API
sections.content:
The RFC groups the APIs into two categories. The Basic (delta-based) API changes the filter one source at a time. It covers two kinds of application: Any-Source Multicast, where all sources are accepted by default and individual ones can be turned off and on (exclude mode), and Source-Specific Multicast, where only sources on a list are allowed (include mode).

The Advanced (full-state) API defines a complete filter of zero or more sources and replaces the previous filter with it in one operation. Applications must use it to switch between include and exclude without leaving the group, and should use it for large source lists because changes are made atomically.

Each style exists in an IPv4-specific variant and a protocol-independent one. The IPv4 variants minimize changes to existing IPv4 code and avoid overloading APIs to cover IPv4 interface addresses versus interface indices.
sections.eli5: You can change your list one name at a time, or hand over a whole new list at once. The one-at-a-time way is simple; the whole-list way is needed for big changes.

sections.title: The Basic Socket Options
sections.content:
The basic API uses setsockopt() options, and using them with getsockopt() gives EOPNOTSUPP. For IPv4, the any-source options are IP_ADD_MEMBERSHIP, IP_BLOCK_SOURCE, IP_UNBLOCK_SOURCE and IP_DROP_MEMBERSHIP. Blocking is meant for cases like a user muting a source, and unblocking undoes it. The source-specific options are IP_ADD_SOURCE_MEMBERSHIP and IP_DROP_SOURCE_MEMBERSHIP; IP_DROP_MEMBERSHIP also drops all joined sources for a group and interface.

The protocol-independent options use struct group_req and struct group_source_req, which carry an interface index and a sockaddr_storage that can hold IPv4 or IPv6 addresses. That lets an application resolve a DNS name to a multicast address of either family and join it.

Errors: EADDRNOTAVAIL when the option is legal but an address is invalid (for example, blocking an already blocked source); EINVAL when the option itself is not legal on the group (mixing source-specific and any-source options); and ENOBUFS if an implementation limit on sources would be exceeded.
sections.eli5: Each button has a name, like join, mute, unmute or leave. Press the wrong one at the wrong time and the computer says why it did not work.

sections.title: Setting and Getting a Full Filter
sections.content:
The full-state API uses new functions: setipv4sourcefilter() and getipv4sourcefilter() for IPv4, and setsourcefilter() and getsourcefilter() for any family. Each takes a socket, an interface, the group, a filter mode (MCAST_INCLUDE or MCAST_EXCLUDE), a source count and a source list. Success returns 0, and failure returns -1 with errno set.

When getting a filter, numsrc on input is the number of addresses that fit in the list and on output is the total number of sources in the filter. If the size is unknown, the application can guess (for example 0) and repeat the call with a bigger buffer if the returned count is larger. Appendix A documents the older ioctl forms, such as SIOCGIPMSFILTER and SIOCSIPMSFILTER, as historic.
sections.eli5: To swap your whole list, you give the computer the new list and say whether it means only these or everyone except these. To read your list, you hand over a box, and it tells you if the box was too small.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says source filtering can help to combat denial-of-service attacks, but is not a complete solution because it does not protect against a spoofed source address that matches an allowed source. Multicast routing protocols that use reverse-path forwarding on the source address offer some natural protection, since a router drops a packet arriving on an interface other than the one toward the real source, but this still does not guarantee protection.
sections.eli5: A guest list helps, but someone could still pretend to be a name on the list.
